summary: This is a genuinely strong, specific skill that captures real expert-level thinking about the intersection of job search mechanics and immigration timelines. It avoids most generic career advice traps by grounding recommendations in specific data (USCIS Employer Data Hub, TEER codes, LCA wage levels, approval rate spreads) and clearly differentiating US and Canada frameworks — a differentiation most generic advice botches. Minor weaknesses: some statistics lack sourcing/dating, and a few sections could go deeper on execution specifics (e.g., what a good cold email actually looks like).
strengths: The 'two clocks running in parallel' framing in Expert Framing is genuinely non-obvious and reframes the entire strategic problem — 'A good job that doesn't advance the immigration timeline is a strategic failure; a mediocre role that does can be the right call' is the kind of counterintuitive insight that separates expert from novice thinking.

The US/Canada differentiation is handled with rare precision. The point that '22% of Canadian employers misunderstand PGWP and self-eliminate' and the heuristic to proactively state 'I have an open work permit — no employer action required' is highly specific and directly actionable — most career advice conflates these markets.

Heuristic #6 ('If a sponsor asks you to pay any H-1B fees, exit immediately... illegal under INA §212(n)') and #7 ('14 months as a Costco cashier is legal PGWP employment and zero CEC-eligible hours simultaneously') are exactly the kind of specific, high-stakes, non-obvious rules that give the skill real teeth.

The Hidden Tradeoffs table is genuinely hidden — e.g., 'Level I wage H-1B filing: 34.2% RFE rate vs. 6.8% at Level IV; the employer's cost saving becomes your immigration risk' is a tradeoff invisible to anyone without insider knowledge.
weaknesses: Several precise-sounding statistics (12.7% denial rate, 38.8% RFE rate, 97.4% vs. 60-75% approval spread, 28,277 employers, 22% employer misunderstanding of PGWP) are stated without date-stamping or source citation within the skill. If any of these are stale or approximated, the AI will confidently repeat them. A 'data currency' note or 'verify current figures' caveat is missing.

The cold outreach section says 'personalize with a specific reference to something the recipient did' and 'keep it under 150 words' but doesn't include even one example of a good vs. bad cold email. Given how central cold outreach is to the funnel logic, the absence of a template or contrast example is a meaningful gap.

The diagnostic framework is strong on triage but light on how to handle mixed/ambiguous cases — e.g., a user on OPT considering both US body-shop and Canadian PGWP paths simultaneously. Step 2 classifications are presented as mutually exclusive when real users often straddle categories.

Visa disclosure timing — mentioned in the description as covered — gets less attention than it deserves. There's a failure pattern about disclosing 'in the first cold email' but no guidance on the actual right moment (post-interview? offer stage? screening call?), which is one of the highest-frequency questions in this domain.
improvement_suggestions: Add a short 'Cold Email Anatomy' subsection with a concrete before/after example — one generic template email and one properly personalized version — showing the 150-word structure, the specific-reference opener, and the 20-minute conversation ask. This is the highest-leverage tactical addition.

Add explicit guidance on WHEN to disclose visa status in the pipeline: not in cold outreach, not in the application, not in first screen, but at a specified point (e.g., after mutual interest is established, before final round, or when directly asked). Include the exact phrasing to use.

Date-stamp the statistics ('FY2025 USCIS data') consistently and add a heuristic like 'Re-verify approval rates and lottery cycle rules against USCIS.gov before advising — H-1B rules change annually.' This protects against stale data as the skill ages.

Add a section or heuristic on handling the OPT 90-day unemployment clock specifically — it's mentioned once in the junior/senior table but deserves standalone treatment since it's a hard legal deadline that produces panic decisions (which the skill correctly warns against but doesn't fully equip the user to avoid).

Consider adding a heuristic on how to evaluate a startup/small company's sponsorship claims — since 70% of petitions come from employers filing ≤100/year, users need a way to assess a first-time or low-volume sponsor's likelihood of following through.
generic_advice_flags: 'Every response should reference the user's specific timeline and constraint — not generic best practices for a hypothetical international student.' This is meta-instruction to the AI rather than domain content; it's correct but boilerplate and doesn't add domain expertise.

'What industry? Tech has year-round rolling hiring; finance/consulting have fixed fall recruiting; biotech, policy, non-tech require industry-specific timing.' The industries beyond tech/finance are lumped as 'industry-specific' without any actual specifics — this is a placeholder more than guidance.
missing_coverage: STEM OPT-specific employer requirements (E-Verify enrollment, formal training plan/I-983, wage requirements) — these disqualify many small employers and are a common surprise late in the process.
Day 1 CPT programs and the resume/immigration risks they create — a highly common trap for students facing OPT expiry who take enrollment in a questionable master's program as a bridge.
Handling the transition FROM PGWP when it's expiring without CEC eligibility yet — bridge options (LMIA, Global Talent Stream, provincial nomination) at a job-search-tactics level.
Cap-gap extension mechanics for F-1 students whose H-1B was selected but not yet activated — a common source of employer confusion that job seekers must proactively explain.
How to evaluate and respond to 'we'll sponsor after X months' verbal promises, which are legally unenforceable and a frequent bait-and-switch pattern.
LinkedIn/resume signaling — whether to list visa status, 'authorized to work' language choices, and how these affect ATS and recruiter filtering.
